prize_parts.citation: For the development of sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry, based on reversible fluorescent terminators and clonally amplified surface clusters, that made massively parallel DNA sequencing possible

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B041 to B017, with Balasubramanian and Klenerman. Nothing in round 1 weakened the zeolite science, but the exchange showed me that B041 is a field rather than a single discovery: Brzezinski and Somfai both said they cannot name the decisive advance, and I had already conceded the same in my own case against. B017 is the opposite: a defined chemical invention (reversible terminators, fluorescent nucleotides, surface-bound templates) that turned a reaction into a digital readout, confirmed on independent platforms for two decades, and with consequences in every area of biology and medicine. Five of eight members put it in their preferred configuration, and none argued that it is immature or scientifically thin. I judge it on the evidence rather than the count, and the evidence is strong. I prefer the two-name Cambridge set because the integrated terminator chemistry and the working platform are the part of the record that is documented and not disputed. A third name would need priority evidence that this committee has not seen.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point. Mayer (cluster concept), Ju (terminator chemistry) and Rothberg (pyrosequencing and semiconductor sequencing) have real claims, and a two-name prize leaves out people whom many regard as pioneers, with the 454 lineage excluded entirely. Sanger and Gilbert were recognised in 1980, so some will read this as a scale-up of known nucleotide chemistry, and much of the impact belongs to biology and medicine. The citation must therefore say plainly that the recognised achievement is the chemistry. Finally, my own field proximity may make me too ready to value a mature, structure-verified chemical story, and I have to guard against that when judging B017 as well.

responses.point: Aili would support Balasubramanian and Klenerman, would not oppose Mayer if the cluster idea proves decisive, and wants the citation to say explicitly that this is chemistry and not a medicine prize.
responses.response: In round 1 I asked why Ju and Rothberg fall outside the citation, and you have partly answered it: the reversible-terminator and cluster chemistry is the line that became the dominant platform, while pyrosequencing and Ju's terminators are distinct routes. I now support the Cambridge pair on that basis. I agree the citation must name the chemistry, which is why mine specifies reversible fluorescent terminators and clonally amplified clusters. Like you, I would not close the door on Mayer, but I would only add him on documented experimental priority, not on the concept alone.

responses.point: Aqvist wants Mayer as a third laureate because clonal clustering made the chemistry scale, but accepts the Cambridge pair alone as the cleaner fallback.
responses.response: The cluster argument is chemically sound, since without clonal amplification on a surface the terminator chemistry would not give massively parallel output. My difficulty is the one Chabes also raised: whether Mayer's work was demonstrated experimentally and independently, or whether it was realised in the Cambridge group. I cannot defend a third name on that record. Because you yourself name the pair as the cleaner fallback, I propose we settle on two names, and I would revisit only if the committee's own priority review shows Mayer's clustering was experimentally independent.

responses.point: Brzezinski proposes a two-part prize pairing B017 (Balasubramanian and Klenerman) with nitrogenase structure credited to Rees alone, and admits the two parts have no obvious joint motivation.
responses.response: I agree with the B017 half and with limiting any nitrogenase citation to structure and cofactor composition, since the mechanism is still debated. I do not support the second part. A Rees-only citation leaves out Dean, Seefeldt, Einsle and Ribbe, whose work on the carbide and cofactor biosynthesis is central to the present picture, and you concede that the pairing reads as a compromise. As the structural chemist here I respect the crystallography, but I would not give a prize part to a structure while the question of how N2 binds is open. I think a single clean B017 prize is stronger than a two-part prize with no shared motivation.

responses.point: Somfai calls the zeolite case broad but diffuse, names no single decisive chemical advance in B041, and says he could support Balasubramanian and Klenerman as his second choice.
responses.response: You are right about B041, and it is a main reason I moved. I could not name one discovery that fits three seats as cleanly as your B048, and Yu and Tsapatsis complicate the cut. On B048 I still hold that its attribution is the cleanest and that 2010 does not make it redundant, so I keep it as an alternative. Your own second choice lies in B017, and the two-name Cambridge set is where you and I now agree. I see the Sanger precedent as a point for the citation wording to address, and not a reason to rank sequencing below a method used mainly by synthetic chemists.

uncertainties: Whether Mayer's clustering contribution has experimental priority that justifies a third seat, and how the exclusion of Ju and Rothberg should be explained in the citation.
Whether the committee will accept sequencing by synthesis as a new chemical capability and not a scale-up of the work honoured in 1980.
Whether B041 or B048 would have been the better choice for a second part if the committee wants one, and how to give two unrelated parts a joint motivation.
statement.conflict_note: I keep my disclosure that my field (electron crystallography of zeolites, MOFs and porous materials) is close to B041, and also to B060 and B018. This is field proximity only, with no personal or institutional tie to Corma, Davis or Zones, and since I no longer prefer B041 it does not bear on my proposed configuration. I have no tie to Balasubramanian, Klenerman or any other B017 candidate. I am a Stockholm University colleague of Secretary Peter Brzezinski, which is not a recusal issue, and no member reports a recusal.
